q1.directions: Use the passage below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Describe ONE reason why European powers were weakened after World War II in ways that encouraged decolonization.
parts.b: Explain ONE way in which colonized peoples themselves contributed to decolonization, using the historian's interpretation in the passage.
parts.c: Explain ONE way in which the Cold War affected the process of decolonization.

sample_answers.a: The war bankrupted Britain and France, destroyed their military capacity, and left them dependent on American aid — making the cost of suppressing colonial revolts unsustainable while their empires no longer paid for themselves.
sample_answers.b: According to the passage, nationalist movements organized mass protests, strikes, and armed resistance that made colonies ungovernable; leaders like Nkrumah, Ho Chi Minh, and Gandhi mobilized populations the Europeans could no longer control by force alone.
sample_answers.c: The United States and Soviet Union both pressured Europeans to decolonize (for different reasons — America to open markets, the USSR to win allies), while superpower rivalry gave nationalist leaders leverage to extract concessions by threatening to align with the other side.

q1.stimulus:
Historians explain the wave of decolonization after 1945 as the result of European weakness meeting colonial resistance. World War II shattered the economic and military foundations of the British, French, and Dutch empires: their cities were bombed, their treasuries empty, and their moral authority damaged by the spectacle of Europeans slaughtering each other while preaching civilization. At the same time, nationalist movements that had been organizing for decades — in India, Indochina, Africa, and the Middle East — seized the moment, using strikes, boycotts, and armed struggle to make continued colonial rule impossibly costly. The Cold War accelerated the process: both superpowers found it useful to champion independence, the Americans to pry open closed colonial markets and the Soviets to recruit allies against the West.
—Historian's account of decolonization in the period c. 1900–present

q2.directions: Use the passage below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Identify ONE goal Nkrumah sets for independent Ghana.
parts.b: Describe ONE way in which Nkrumah connects Ghana's independence to the broader African continent.
parts.c: Explain ONE reason why Nkrumah emphasizes that independence must be followed by continued struggle.

sample_answers.a: Nkrumah declares that Ghana's independence is meaningless unless it is linked to the total liberation of Africa, committing the new nation to support independence movements across the continent.
sample_answers.b: He argues that Ghana is not truly free while other Africans remain colonized, presenting Ghana's independence as the first step in a continent-wide liberation rather than a purely national achievement.
sample_answers.c: Nkrumah warns that political independence alone does not end economic exploitation; he feared that without continued unity and effort, the former colonial powers would maintain control through economic pressure — what he later called neocolonialism.

q2.stimulus:
At long last, the battle has ended. Ghana, our beloved country, is free forever. We have won the battle, but the struggle is not yet over — for our independence is meaningless unless it is linked up with the total liberation of the African continent. Let us now, as a people, set ourselves to the task of building a new nation, strong and united. We must learn to live as Africans, and we must show the world that we are capable of managing our own affairs. Forward ever, backward never.
—Adapted from Kwame Nkrumah's speech at Ghana's independence ceremony, 6 March 1957

q3.directions: Use the map below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Describe ONE pattern shown on the map regarding the timing of African independence.
parts.b: Explain ONE cause of the rapid wave of African independence around 1960.
parts.c: Explain ONE difference between the decolonization of British and French Africa as reflected in the independence dates.

sample_answers.a: The map shows a concentrated wave of independence around 1960 — the 'Year of Africa' — when more than a dozen French and British colonies became independent within months of each other, after earlier independence in places like Ghana (1957) and later liberation in southern Africa.
sample_answers.b: France's defeat in Algeria and Britain's inability to afford colonial wars, combined with organized nationalist parties demanding self-rule and international pressure at the UN, made continued colonial rule untenable; both powers chose negotiated withdrawal over costly repression.
sample_answers.c: Most French colonies became independent in a coordinated wave in 1960 when de Gaulle offered a referendum on independence, while British decolonization was more staggered (Ghana 1957, Nigeria 1960, Kenya 1963), reflecting Britain's case-by-case negotiations.

q3.stimulus: The map shows the dates of independence for African nations, with each country labeled by the year it became independent. The pattern reveals a dramatic concentration in the early 1960s: Ghana (1957) led the way, followed by a wave in 1960 when numerous French colonies and Nigeria gained independence, with most of the continent independent by the mid-1960s and only southern Africa (such as Zimbabwe in 1980 and Namibia in 1990) remaining under colonial or white-minority rule into later decades.
